The development of sustainable energy storage devices relies
heavily on electrode materials with both high performance and
cost-effectiveness. Biomass-derived porous activated carbons
(ACs) have emerged as attractive candidates because of their
wide availability and affordability. However, they often exhibit
insufficient hierarchical porosity and limited electrochemical per-
formance, necessitating further optimization. Herein, we report
a facile and effective strategy to synthesize porous AC from
waste rice straw (RS) and systematically investigate the effects
of activation temperature, ratio, and sequence. The optimized
AC prepared at 900 °C with a 1:4 activation ratio exhibits a
hierarchical porous structure and a specific surface area (SSA)
of 694.05 m2 g−1. It delivers a high specific capacitance of
128.6 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 and excellent rate capability in 6 M
KOH using a three-electrode system. Additionally, the symmetric
supercapacitor shows superior cycling stability, retaining 96.6%
capacitance after 5000 cycles. These results demonstrate that
RS is a promising precursor for porous AC, and that an opti-
mized activation strategy can successfully achieve the desired
hierarchical pore structure, thereby significantly enhancing the
electrochemical performance. This study provides a sustainable
and cost-effective pathway for converting agricultural waste
into high-value electrode materials for future energy storage
applications.

Abstract
Molybdenum disulfide  (MoS2), as a representative transition-metal sulfide, exhibits high capacity for  Li+ storage processes. 
However, its large volume expansion and low conductivity during  Li+ storage result in poor cycling stability and insufficient 
fast-charging performance, severely limiting its practical applications. Here, an atomic-level stacked structure consisting of 
Ni-doped  MoS2 and carbon layers is fabricated. The stacked structure maximizes the intimate atomic-scale interfacial contact 
between  MoS2 and carbon layers, improves the structural stability of  MoS2 during  Li+ storage, and enhances its electronic 
conductivity. Ni doping transforms the semiconductor properties of  MoS2 into metallic properties and simultaneously reduces 
its  Li+ transport energy barrier, thus enhancing its charge transport capability. More interestingly, ex situ transmission electron 
microscopy and in situ magnetometry reveal that the doped Ni atoms can convert into superparamagnetic Ni nanoparticles 
during discharge, which serve as carriers to store electrons and facilitate the storage of  Li+ in  Li2S. The process induces 
a spin-polarized surface capacitance effect at the interfaces between Ni and  Li2S, enhancing the storage and transport of 
 Li+. As a result, the composite material delivers high  Li+ storage capacity, superior stability, and excellent fast-charging 
capability in both coin-type half-cells and Ah-level pouch full cells. This work first confirms the enhancement mechanism 
of spin-polarized surface capacitance effect in the  Li+ storage performance of  MoS2, providing insights for advancing high-
performance  MoS2-based lithium battery anodes.

ABSTRACT
Lignin, the most abundant renewable aromatic biopolymer, is increasingly recognized as a versatile precursor for 
functional environmental materials. This Perspective proposes a chemistry-dimension-function-lifetime frame -
work that links the extraction-dependent heterogeneity of technical lignins, chemical modification, and multi -
scale material architectures (0D – 3D) to environmental functions in sorption, photocatalysis, and sensing. Distinct 
technical lignins derived from different extraction routes exhibit diverse functional groups, interunit linkages, 
molecular-weight distributions, and condensation degrees, which govern their transformation into materials such 
as nanoparticles, fibers, membranes, hydrogels, and aerogels with controlled morphologies, thereby regulating 
kinetics, mass transport, interfacial accessibility, stability, and lifetime. Chemical modification strategies, 
including carboxylation, amination, and sulfonation, enhance adsorption capacity, selectivity, and regeneration 
for heavy metals and organic pollutants, highlighting lignin functionalities as key design parameters for envi -
ronmental remediation. Beyond adsorption, lignin's conjugated aromatic structure enables intrinsic photo -
activity, supporting light-driven degradation pathways in catalytic hybrids, thereby coupling adsorption and 
photoredox reactivity. With emerging AI-guided design, lignin-derived carbon dots and composite materials 
further extend functionality toward optical and electrical sensing of volatile organic compounds and metal ions.

In response to increasingly severe energy crises and environmental pollution, converting plant/seed shell waste

apricot shells. Building on this classification, the paper reveals how material properties decisively influence the 
development of active carbon pores and surface chemistry. The paper emphasizes comparing the mechanism 
differences among various shells under identical modification strategies, identifying optimal modification
